1.pericope_label: The Corinthians’ letter, the good of celibacy, and the mutual right of husband and wife

schools.summary: Gill notes that for all the influence of the false apostles many at Corinth still kept up a correspondence with Paul and deferred greatly to his judgment, and that the questions they asked may be collected from the contents of this chapter and those following, whether a Christian ought to abstain from the use of women, whether a believer ought to live with an unbelieving yoke-fellow, and the like; he takes the advice about marriage as meant to prevent unlawful commerce of every kind, observes that the Syriac renders the word for the husband’s duty as due love, which takes in all the offices of tenderness, care and protection, and holds that the phrase is here a euphemism for the marriage duty proper. Calvin says that the Corinthians’ consulting Paul shows they retained some respect for him notwithstanding the scattered state of the church, though what they asked is uncertain except so far as the reply discloses it; he turns the opening verdict against a later abuse, that soon after the first rise of the Church there crept in by Satan’s artifice a superstition which, through a foolish admiration of celibacy, despised the sacred connection of marriage. The command to marry he restricts to those who feel themselves urged by necessity, of which every man must judge for himself, those who have the gift of abstinence being left at liberty; and he lays down the general doctrine of mutual benevolence, asking why the apostle puts husband and wife on a level here instead of requiring obedience of the wife.

Henry treats the apostle as a faithful and skilful casuist answering cases of conscience which the Corinthians had proposed, and observes that as the lips of ministers should keep knowledge so the people should ask the law at their mouths. He limits the good of not touching a woman to that juncture of time at least, and denies that good here means what is so conformable to the mind and will of God that to do otherwise were sin, marriage being the remedy God had appointed against the fornication he had warned them of in the previous chapter.

Clarke calls the husband’s obligation the matrimonial debt or conjugal duty, which husband and wife must take care mutually to render, since where it is withheld alienation of affection is the infallible consequence, and this in numberless instances has led to adulterous connections, so that in such cases the wife has herself to blame for the infidelity of her husband; he supports the sense of the word rendered fornication from a passage of Hosea where the prophet threatens married people with the loss of children, and observes that neither husband nor wife has authority to refuse what the other has a matrimonial right to demand. Wesley reads the opening verdict of the man who is master of himself, so great and many being the advantages of a single life, notes that the words his own wife exclude polygamy since Christianity allows none, and bids no one forget the mutual right on pretence of greater purity.

Barnes marks the formal division, since the chapter begins the second part of the epistle, the discussion of points submitted to the apostle in a letter from the church at Corinth which has since been lost and which, if we had it, would throw light on the answers; he praises the delicacy of the language about the marriage duty, the expression being removed as far as possible from the grossness of heathen writers, since the word used denotes kindness and good-will while the word due recalls the sacredness of the vow, and he adds that Paul would keep the church from scandal. Ellicott renders the reason for marrying as because of the prevalent fornication, so general at Corinth and so little accounted sin that the unmarried were liable to be led into it, and concedes that the apostle may seem at first to put marriage on very low and merely utilitarian ground, answering that he writes with a definite and limited aim and sets out the higher aspects of matrimony elsewhere; he prefers the reading of the better manuscripts, her due, takes the verse as answering the scruples of those already married who doubted whether they should continue so, and finds with Bengel an elegant paradox in the saying that she has not power of her own body. Robertson supplies the ellipsis of the opening from the papyri, warns that the questions must be clearly before us if the replies are to be intelligently read, insists that Paul says a single life is not wrong but good while denying that he opposes marriage, since a mark of certain heretics will be the forbidding to marry, and holds that the reason given is a true one but not the only one, the main purpose of marriage being children and mutual love another; in wedlock, he says, separate ownership of the person ceases, and this dictum defends marital intercourse against rigorists as the first verse commends celibacy against sensualists. Lightfoot sets the verse against the rabbinic rule, where marriage is enjoined under a severe command laid on the man and not the woman from his sixteenth or seventeenth year, so that by exceeding twenty he makes an affirmative precept void, unless he is studious in the law and fears that the care of a wife would hinder his study, in which case he may still tarry.

Chrysostom explains the turn in the letter: having corrected the three heaviest things laid to their charge, the distraction of the Church, the fornicator and the covetous man, Paul thenceforth uses a milder sort of speech and interposes some exhortation and advice about marriage and virginity, giving his hearers some respite from more unpleasant subjects, whereas in the second epistle he does the contrary, beginning from the milder topics and ending with the more distressing, not setting all down in regular order but varying his discourse as the occasion and the exigency of the matters required.

debates: What the opening verdict concedes: Robertson insists that Paul calls the single life good without calling marriage wrong, and warns that a mark of certain heretics will be the forbidding to marry; Henry limits the good to that juncture of time; Calvin turns the verse against the superstition which afterwards despised marriage out of a foolish admiration of celibacy; and Lightfoot sets it against the rabbinic rule which enjoined marriage under a severe command

Whether marriage is here placed on merely utilitarian ground: Ellicott concedes the appearance and answers from the limited aim of the passage, Robertson denies it outright and names children and mutual love as the true purposes, and Calvin restricts the command to those urged by necessity while leaving the continent at liberty
outliers: Chrysostom observes that the order of this epistle is the reverse of the second, which begins with the milder topics and ends with the more distressing
Lightfoot records the rabbinic exemption by which a man studious in the law, who fears that a wife would hinder his study, may tarry past the age at which marriage was commanded
Clarke warns that where the marriage duty is withheld the injured party is not the only one to blame for what follows

5.pericope_label: Defraud not one another: the temporary separation, the permission, and the gift of continence

schools.summary: Gill calls the withholding of the marriage duty a piece of injustice and properly a defrauding, since both parties have a right to it, while allowing that under the conditions named it may be lawful for married persons to lie apart. He excludes from the permission the two things that are commands, that every man should have his own wife and that husband and wife should render what is due to each other, and refers it instead to their parting for a time and coming together again; and on the apostle’s wish he holds that Paul speaks not of his own state, married or unmarried, which cannot be determined, but of the gift of continency, which he desires for all men that they may be out of the way of Satan’s temptations and the fitter for the service of Christ. Calvin defends the plainness of the passage: profane persons might think Paul wanting in modesty to discourse so of the intercourse of husband and wife, or think it beneath the dignity of an apostle, but he was under necessity, knowing how much a false appearance of sanctity can beguile devout minds, since Satan dazzles us with a show of what is right until we imagine ourselves polluted by intercourse with our own wives and think of leaving our calling for another kind of life. He draws from the verse about the gift the conclusion that had the passage been duly weighed, the perverse superstition attached to the desire of celibacy, which is the root and cause of great evils, would never have gained a footing in the world.

Clarke holds that the separations permitted here, for the apostle enjoins none, are only for a season and on extraordinary occasions, and that the parties may come together again lest Satan take advantage; he supplies the background of the permission from the rabbins, the more conscientious of whom made a constant distinction between what they enjoined on their own judgment and what they built on the authority of the law; and he ties the apostle’s wish to the necessities of the Church and what is afterwards called the present distress, since it could never be Paul’s wish that marriage should cease among men or that the Church should always be composed of single persons, which would be equally absurd, though while the Church was in straits it was much better for its single members not to encumber themselves. Wesley makes the occasions of separation special and solemn ones on which husband and wife may give themselves up entirely to the exercises of devotion, warns that if they remain long apart Satan will tempt them to unclean thoughts if not to actions too, refers the permission to the separating for a time and the coming together again with a possible glance at the earlier verse, and thinks Paul had tasted the sweetness of that liberty and wished others to enjoy it, ending where our Lord ended, that all men cannot receive this saying save those to whom it is given.

Barnes insists that even by mutual consent the apostle would not have the separation perpetual, since it would expose them to the very evils the marriage relation was designed to avoid, and that Satan is not to be given the advantage of throwing them into temptation. On the permission he admits that it is not certain whether the word refers back or forward, that commentators are divided, and that while the more natural construction looks backward to the preceding verse, recent writers refer it to what follows and Calvin to the opening verse; and he denies that Paul would prefer all men unmarried, which would be against the divine institution and against his own precepts elsewhere, making the wish one for such control of the passions as the apostle himself had. Ellicott turns the verse about prayer into a piece of textual history, since the alteration of the Greek verb into the present tense, so as to make the prayer refer to daily devotions rather than to special and exceptional seasons, together with the interpolation of the word fasting which the older manuscripts do not have, is a striking example of the way the ascetic tendencies of a particular ecclesiastical school led them to amend the sacred text; he would render the next verse, I say this as a permission and not as a command, and warns that the English as it stands might seem to make the apostle claim only a permission to write, whereas his meaning is that the foregoing instructions are not absolute commands but general permissive instruction to be applied by each according to circumstances; and he puts the wish as one that all had the same grace of continence, so that they might remain unmarried without risk of sin, adding that there are many gifts and God has given each man his own. Robertson notes that the verb of the separation means to have leisure, from the noun that gives us our word school, and that the tense makes it a single act and not a settled condition, the private devotions here being worth marking, while the clause about the tempter is a present subjunctive, that Satan may not keep on tempting them; he glosses the word for permission as knowing together, understanding, agreement and so concession, concludes that Paul has not commanded people to marry but has left it an open question, and takes the wish to prove that Paul was not then married, adding that whether he had been married and was now a widower turns on how his casting of a vote is understood, which there is no way to decide.

debates: What the permission covers: Barnes admits the reference is uncertain and inclines backward while recording that recent writers look forward and Calvin to the opening verse, Gill excludes the plain commands and refers it to the temporary parting, and Ellicott takes it of the leading thought of the whole passage while warning that the English rendering misstates the apostle’s claim

How far the wish that all were as Paul extends: Barnes and Ellicott confine it to the gift of continence and deny that he would have all men unmarried, Clarke ties it to the present distress and calls the alternative absurd, and Calvin makes the verse the standing refutation of enforced celibacy
outliers: Ellicott charges an ascetic school of churchmen with amending the text here, both by changing the tense of the verb and by inserting the word fasting, which the older manuscripts lack
Robertson derives our word school from the verb Paul uses for having leisure to pray
Clarke cites the rabbinic practice of marking off what was enjoined on private judgment from what rested on the authority of the law

8.pericope_label: To the unmarried and the widows: better to marry than to burn

schools.summary: Gill takes the unmarried for either those who never married or those whose wives are dead, and prefers the second sense because widows are joined with them; he draws from the permission the corollary that second marriages are lawful, which some of the ancients condemned, and takes the burning of the fire of lust itself, neither the material fire with which Judah would have had Tamar burnt nor the hell fire such uncleanness deserves. Calvin ties the advice to what precedes, since the gifts of God are variously distributed and continency is not in every man’s power, so that an unmarried life ought to be desired by those who can bear it, provided each measures himself by his own measure. At the following words he turns sharply: while he advises abstinence Paul always speaks conditionally, but where the infirmity of the flesh will not allow that liberty he enjoins marriage as a thing not in the least doubtful, and says it so that no one may take it for mere advice; nor is it only fornicators that he restrains but those also who are defiled in the sight of God by inward lust, and a man who neglects the remedy of marriage tempts God, so that the matter requires not advice but strict prohibition. He denies too that there is strictly a comparison in the closing clause, since marriage is lawful while the other thing is exceedingly wrong, the apostle having used a customary form of expression.

Clarke holds that the apostle speaks here of men who had been married and were now widowers, and that in saying even as I he means that he was one himself, several of the ancients ranking Paul among the married apostles. On the burning he reports Bishop Pearce’s rendering, that it is better to marry than to be made uneasy, since the verb means primarily to burn but metaphorically to be troubled or vexed, as where the apostle asks who is offended and he burns not; he thinks it well to soften the sense of the word and denies that Paul can mean burning with lust, any more than Virgil does in saying that the unfortunate Dido burns. Wesley holds that Paul was then single beyond doubt and that the history makes it probable he always was, and adds that this declaration has no reference at all to a state of persecution.

Barnes allows the word unmarried either sense and says it here means simply those who were then unmarried, the reasoning applying to both, adding that widows are specified where widowers are not because the never-married are treated more particularly at the end of the chapter; the passion of the closing clause he says is often compared to a fire, and holds it better to marry, with all the inconveniences of married life in a time of distress and persecution, than to be the prey of raging and consuming passions. Ellicott explains the pairing of widows with the unmarried as a precaution, since otherwise a question might have arisen whether the advice was meant for them at all, calls the conjecture that Paul was a widower, which Luther among others made, a curious one, since it requires the word unmarried to be restricted to widowers, which is quite inadmissible, and holds that even if that were admitted the deduction could scarcely be called logical, the almost universal tradition of the early Church being that Paul was never married; the ground of the comparison he puts plainly, that to be influenced by unlawful desire is a sin while to marry is none. Robertson thinks it possible that by the unmarried only men are meant, since widows are added here and virgins receive separate treatment later, agrees that it is hardly likely Paul means only widowers and widows and means to call himself a widower, notes that Paul has nowhere said celibacy is better than marriage though he has justified it and stated his own preference, and observes that the metaphorical use of the verb for sexual passion is common enough, as it is also for grief. Lightfoot supplies a rabbinic story to the point, of a man who adjured the evil affection to go out of him, whereupon it went out as a pillar of fire, and who said to it, Thou art fire and I am flesh, yet for all that I have prevailed against thee.

Cyril of Jerusalem holds that those who marry but once should not reprobate those who have consented to a second marriage, since continence is a noble and admirable thing and yet it is also permissible to enter upon a second marriage, that the weak may not fall into fornication; all other practices, he adds, are to be banished afar, fornication, adultery and every kind of licentiousness, and the body kept pure for the Lord, that the Lord may have respect unto the body.

debates: Whether Paul was a widower: Clarke takes the words even as I to mean that he was, and reports that several of the ancients ranked him among the married apostles, while Ellicott calls the conjecture curious and inadmissible on lexical grounds and appeals to the almost universal tradition of the early Church, Robertson judges it hardly likely, and Wesley thinks it probable he was never married at all

What the burning means: Clarke follows Bishop Pearce in softening it to being made uneasy and denies that lust can be meant, Gill takes it of the fire of lust itself while excluding both material and hell fire, Barnes and Robertson treat the metaphor as ordinary, and Calvin denies that the clause is strictly a comparison at all
outliers: Lightfoot cites a rabbinic story in which the evil affection, adjured to depart, went out of a man as a pillar of fire, and was told, Thou art fire and I am flesh, yet I have prevailed against thee
Clarke supports his reading of the verb from Virgil’s line about the unfortunate Dido
Cyril of Jerusalem uses the verse to defend second marriages against those who would reproach them

10.pericope_label: To the married, not I but the Lord: the indissoluble tie and the separated wife

schools.summary: Gill marks the change of footing, that to the unmarried and widows Paul spoke by permission and gave counsel, whereas to those already in a married state what he has to say is by commandment, enjoining what they are under obligation to observe and are not at liberty to alter; and he holds that the departure supposed in the next verse is not thereby allowed, being lawful only in the case of fornication. Calvin takes the verse for the indissolubility of the tie and finds in it a condemnation of all those divorces which were of daily occurrence among the heathen and went unpunished among the Jews under the law of Moses. He is surprised that no exception is made even for adultery, since Paul is not likely to have designed to curtail in anything the doctrine of Christ, and concludes that, discoursing of these matters only in passing, the apostle chose rather to send the Corinthians back to the Lord’s own permission and prohibition than to repeat them. At the following verse he adds that what is said cannot apply to those put away for adultery, as the punishment shows, that being a capital crime by the Roman laws and almost by the common law of nations; what he has in view is husbands who divorced their wives because their manners were not congenial or their appearance did not please them, and wives who deserted their husbands on account of cruelty or dishonourable treatment, and against all such he holds that marriage is not dissolved by divorces or dissensions.

Henry supplies the occasion, since the question must have been frequent in that age and especially among the Jewish converts whether they were to live with heathen relatives in a married state: the law of Moses permitted divorce, and there was a famous instance in the Jewish state when the people were obliged to put away their idolatrous wives, which might well move a scruple in many minds whether converts to Christianity were not bound to put away or desert mates who continued unbelieving. To that the apostle answers in general that marriage, by Christ’s command, is for life, so that those who are married must not think of separation, the wife not departing from the husband nor the husband putting away the wife.

Clarke says the apostle does not give his own private opinion or judgment here, since the Lord Jesus has commanded that man shall not put asunder what God has joined, and God had said the same at the beginning; he fills in the background from the Jewish side, where the marriage bond was held very loosely, a woman being able to put away her husband by declaring before the elders that her mother or her brethren had wedded her too young and that she would not have him, and receiving a certificate accordingly, and he notes that among the Jews the wife had just as much right to put away her husband as the husband to put away his wife, which served as a mutual check. Divorces, he holds, cannot be allowed but in the case of fornication, an act of that kind dissolving the marriage vow while nothing else can; the woman who departs does so at her own peril and must either remain unmarried or be reconciled. Wesley reads the disclaimer as not I only but Christ, by his express command, and excepts the cause of adultery from the prohibition laid on the husband.

Ellicott denies outright that the contrast is between commands given by St Paul as an inspired apostle and St Paul as a private individual, since he expressly claims elsewhere that all his commands as an apostle are to be regarded as the commandments of the Lord, and speaks of the knowledge into which the Spirit guided him as given by the word of the Lord; on the following verse he renders it, if she have actually separated, treats the intervening words as a parenthesis and the clause about the husband as the completion of the Lord’s command, and holds that the apostle anticipates the difficult question by remarking that such a woman must not marry again but ought to be reunited to her former husband. Barnes insists that the injunction is not to be understood as advice merely but as a solemn divine command from which they are not at liberty to depart, and supposes the following rule aimed at wives who, ignorant of the rule of Christ and supposing they had a right to separate themselves, had rashly done so and thought the marriage contract dissolved: they must either be reconciled or remain alone, the tie being too sacred to be dissolved by the will of either party. Robertson gives the plain account of the disclaimer, that Paul had no word of Jesus about the unmarried while Jesus had spoken plainly to the married about divorce, so that Paul reinforces his own inspired command by the Master’s; he observes that Paul makes no allowance here for the remarriage of the innocent party as Jesus does by implication, and glosses the verb for being reconciled as an old compound for exchanging coins of equal value, one of Paul’s great words for reconciliation with God. Lightfoot sets the disclaimer beside the distinction usual in the rabbinic schools between producing a text of Scripture and producing an opinion.

debates: What the disclaimer not I but the Lord concedes: Ellicott denies that it distinguishes Paul as apostle from Paul as private man, since he claims elsewhere that all his apostolic commands are the Lord’s; Robertson explains it simply as the presence or absence of a saying of Jesus on the point; Barnes and Wesley read it as adding the Master’s authority to the apostle’s, and Lightfoot compares the rabbinic distinction between a text and an opinion

Whether adultery is an exception here: Calvin is surprised that none is made and concludes that Paul, writing in passing, sent his readers back to Christ’s own words, while denying at the next verse that the separated wife of that case is in view at all; Clarke and Wesley admit fornication as the one dissolving cause, and Robertson notes that Paul allows no remarriage even to the innocent party
outliers: Clarke reproduces the form of words by which a Jewish wife could put away her husband before the elders, and notes that the right was equal on both sides
Robertson derives the verb for being reconciled from the exchanging of coins of equal value

12.pericope_label: To the rest: the mixed marriage, and the sanctifying of the unbelieving partner

schools.summary: Gill explains the disclaimer by the change of persons addressed, since what went before was spoken to those on equal footing in religion, both being believers, whereas here the apostle turns to the unequally yoked, and, no express determination of the Lord’s being extant on the point, gives his own sense of it under divine inspiration, holding such marriages valid and such persons bound to live together and not to separate on account of difference in religion; on the sanctifying he notes that the better reading of the Latin and Syriac is by the believing wife. Calvin sets out the answer in two clauses, that the believing party ought not to withdraw or seek a divorce unless put away, and that if an unbeliever puts away a spouse on account of religion the believer is by that rejection freed from the bond; and he insists that Paul does not mean these regulations are from himself in such a way as not to be from the Lord. The scruple behind the question he states fully: the relationship of marriage is so close, the wife being the half of the man and her husband’s partner in everything, that it seems impossible for a believer to live with an ungodly spouse without being polluted by so close a connection; Paul declares nevertheless that marriage is sacred and pure and that no contagion need be feared, though we should bear in mind that he speaks not of contracting such marriages but of maintaining those already contracted.

Clarke says that for what he had spoken before the apostle had the testimony of the Lord by Moses and of his own Master Christ, while for these directions there is no written testimony and he delivers them now for the first time, which does not intimate that he was not under the influence of the Divine Spirit but only that nothing in the sacred writings bore directly on the point. He puts the first rule plainly, that the husband is not to put his wife away because she still continues in her heathen superstition, and would render the clause about sanctifying as meaning that the unbeliever is to be reputed as sanctified on account of the believing spouse, her sanctity as far as outward things go being imputed to him so as to render their connection not unlawful, the word being applied here much more to the Christian state than to any moral change in the persons, since saints is the common term for those baptized into the faith of Christ. Wesley calls the direction a revelation from God though our Lord left no commandment on the point, meets the obvious precedent by observing that the Jews were of old obliged to put away their idolatrous wives but that their case was quite different, since they were absolutely forbidden to marry such women while the persons here spoken of married when both were in a state of heathenism, and makes the argument from the children an appeal to sight, since otherwise they would have been brought up heathens whereas now they are Christians.

Ellicott marks the new class, since up to this point only Christians have been in view and there remains the case of mixed marriages, of which a church like Corinth must have had many arising from the conversion of only one partner; the words are emphatically of a man who already has a wife, the case of a Christian marrying a heathen not being alluded to here and being forbidden elsewhere. He notes that the same strong verb is used of the woman as of the man, since under Roman law a wife could equally obtain a divorce, and rejects as wholly inadmissible the suggestion that the word is chosen because her being a Christian inverts the natural order and makes her the superior; on the sanctifying he sets this lawful union against that other in which the connection is defiling and holds that the purity of the believing partner entirely overweighs the impurity of the unbeliever, which is not a moral but a kind of ceremonial impurity, adding that the children of such marriages were reckoned Christian children and that the fruit being holy we must regard the tree as holy too, while warning that the holiness meant is not the inward sanctification which springs from faith. Barnes reads the change of phrase practically, since the wife had no power to expel her husband from his own house though she might think separation her duty; she should rather love him and seek his welfare, bearing much and bearing it long that she may win him, and should not leave him unless her life is made miserable or endangered or he leaves her wholly unprovided for. He frames the objection behind the sanctifying as a question, whether one is not defiled in the eye of God by a close union with an enemy of the gospel, and answers that the contrary may be true. Robertson denies that the disclaimer is any disclaimer of inspiration, since Paul means only that he is not quoting a command of Jesus, the problem being a new one thrown up by the work among the Gentiles which did not arise in the Lord’s own time, so that Paul deals with mixed marriages as missionaries do now in heathen lands; he observes that a relative clause stands where a conditional one stood before, Paul being perfectly fair in stating both sides, denies that Paul means the unbelieving husband is saved by the faith of his wife, though Hodge actually so interprets him, and supplies the ellipsis about the children, that since it is otherwise they are illegitimate.

debates: What the disclaimer I, not the Lord concedes: Robertson denies that it disclaims inspiration and makes it simply the absence of a saying of Jesus on a question that had not yet arisen, Clarke that there was nothing in the sacred writings bearing directly on the point, Wesley calls it revelation without a commandment of the Lord, and Calvin insists that what is from Paul is not therefore not from the Lord

In what sense the unbelieving partner is sanctified: Robertson rules out salvation by the faith of the other and names Hodge as reading it so, Clarke makes it a reputed and outward sanctity belonging to the Christian state rather than a moral change, Ellicott makes the impurity overweighed a ceremonial and not a moral one, and Calvin restricts the whole ruling to marriages already contracted
outliers: Ellicott rejects the reading which would make the believing wife the superior partner and so explain the stronger verb used of her
Barnes sets practical limits to what a Christian wife must bear from an unbelieving husband, naming danger to life and total neglect of provision as the points at which no precept binds her
Robertson remarks that the sense is so simple that one wonders at the ability of men to get confused over Paul’s language

15.pericope_label: If the unbeliever depart: the believer’s liberty, and the hope of saving the other

schools.summary: Gill defines the case as one where the unbelieving party separates on account of religion and in hatred of it, refusing to live with the believer unless Christ is denied, his gospel abjured and his worship relinquished; on the closing question he offers both senses without deciding, the first being that the believer may be easy at the departure, since after all proper means have been tried there is no certainty of doing the other any good. Calvin makes the ground of the liberty strong: the unbelieving party who repudiates a spouse ready to dwell with them makes a divorce with God rather than with the partner, so that here the first and chief bond is not merely loosed but utterly broken through. The closing question he takes as an exhortation drawn from the advantage to be gained, since it is a great and distinguished blessing if a wife win her husband, and unbelievers are not in so hopeless a condition that they cannot be brought to believe, being dead indeed but not beyond the God who raises the dead; so long as any hope of doing good remains, the pious wife should not depart.

Clarke reads the freedom as freedom from any particular laws that would prevent remarriage, and thinks the law probably stood so then though it does not now, since marriage can be dissolved only by death or by the ecclesiastical court, neither fornication nor adultery dissolving the marriage contract and no obstinate separation, however long continued, giving the abandoned party authority to remarry. The closing question he turns into direct counsel, that Christians with heathen partners should not give them up because they are such but should bear their cross and look up to God, who may give the unbelieving husband or wife to their prayers. Wesley says only that the believer is at full liberty and not enslaved, and takes the clause about peace as a charge to live peaceably with them if it be possible.

Barnes says that if the unbeliever chooses to leave you cannot prevent it and must submit patiently and bear it as a Christian; he reports that many have supposed the deserted party free to marry again, Calvin, Grotius and Rosenmuller among them, but holds that contrary to the strain of the argument, taking the sense to be that the one left is not bound by the marriage tie to make provision for the one who departed or to do things prejudicial to religion by a violent effort to retain them. The closing question he reads as a reason why the believing party should not separate needlessly, the possibility, or rather the probability, of the other’s conversion being reason enough for continuing together. Ellicott puts the case as one of conscience, since where the married life is made intolerable by the unbeliever urging the believer to religious acts conscience cannot approve, the earlier commands for continued union do not hold, and adds that this permission is in no way contrary to our Lord’s single ground of divorce, the apostle having already reminded his readers that the Lord’s command does not cover the case. On the closing question he reverses the usual reading: it has generally been taken as modifying what precedes, as though the apostle advised against letting the unbeliever go wherever there was any chance of effecting a conversion, but the true meaning is precisely the opposite, since the remote contingency of the unbeliever’s conversion is too vague a thing for which to risk the peace that is so essential an element of the Christian life. Robertson holds that wilful desertion by the unbeliever sets the other free, a case not contemplated in Christ’s words, and notes that Luther argued the released partner might marry again, though that is by no means clear unless the unbeliever marries first; the call to peace he glosses as a permanent call in the sphere and atmosphere of peace, and on the closing question he concedes that the syntax allows either construction, that the second suits the context best and is adopted by most commentators, while confessing that he hesitates to read Paul as favouring divorce unless the unbeliever strongly insists, since there is no problem at all unless the unbeliever makes one, and where the case is hopeless acquiescence is the only wise solution.

debates: Whether the deserted believer may marry again: Clarke reads the freedom as freedom to remarry under the law as it then stood while denying that it holds now, Robertson takes wilful desertion to set the other free and reports Luther’s further step without endorsing it, Calvin speaks of the chief bond as utterly broken through, and Barnes denies the inference outright as contrary to the argument and confines the sense to release from providing for the deserter

What the closing question is for: Calvin, Barnes and Clarke take it as a motive for staying, since the hope of winning the other is reason enough to continue together, while Ellicott holds that the true meaning is precisely the opposite, the bare contingency of a conversion being too vague to justify risking the peace God has called us to, and Robertson allows either syntax while leaning to the second and hesitating over it
outliers: Barnes names Calvin, Grotius and Rosenmuller as holding a view of this verse which he then rejects
Robertson reports Luther’s opinion that the released partner may marry again and declines to follow it unless the unbeliever marries first
Clarke sets out the later state of the law, under which neither adultery nor prolonged desertion dissolves the marriage contract

17.pericope_label: As the Lord hath called each: the rule of abiding, and the case of circumcision

schools.summary: Gill notices that the words are so placed and so expressed that they look both ways, back to every man’s proper gift, whether of continence or of disposition to marriage, and forward to what follows; he glosses the calling as the civil calling, station and business of life, and allows that circumcision was once a command and an ordinance given to Abraham and his natural seed, pointing at the corruption of nature and typical of the blood of Christ, while denying that it can make any man righteous in the sight of God or is of any avail in the business of salvation. Calvin makes contentment the substance of the rule, that every one should be satisfied with his calling and pursue it instead of seeking to betake himself to something else, a calling in Scripture meaning a lawful mode of life which has its relation to the God who calls us to this or that. The example of circumcision he thinks designedly chosen to reprove in passing the superstition and haughtiness of the Jews, since men who gloried in circumcision might well feel dissatisfied with the want of it, as though their condition were the worse; Paul therefore places both conditions upon a level, lest through hatred of the one the other should be foolishly desired.

Henry takes the principle at its widest, since our states and circumstances in this world are distributions of divine Providence, which fixes the bounds of men’s habitations and orders their steps, God setting up and pulling down; and whatever a man’s circumstances or condition were when he was converted to Christianity, let him abide in them.

Clarke reads the closing clause of the rule as a disclaimer of favouritism, since Paul lays on the Corinthians no burden which others are not called to bear but a general rule imposed by God’s authority on every Christian society, and bids every man fulfil the duties of the state to which the providence of God has called him; any situation of life, he adds, is equally friendly to the salvation of the soul if a man is faithful to the grace he has received, so that in all situations a Christian should be content, all things working together for good to him who loves God. On the removal of the marks of circumcision he notes that it could be done by art and that Celsus himself prescribes the mode, and he holds that circumcision, though commanded of God, was nothing of itself, being only a sign of the justification afterwards received by faith. Wesley glosses the calling as the outward state and bids a man not seek to change it without a clear direction from Providence, and says that circumcision and uncircumcision will neither promote nor obstruct our salvation, the one point being the keeping of the commandments of God, which is faith working by love.

Ellicott treats the intervening question as a parenthesis, so that this rule follows straight on the permission and limits in practice the very broad liberty just granted, noting that in that permission the unbelieving partner alone is spoken of as taking an active part while the believer merely acquiesces for the sake of peace and is never to cause or promote a separation. Over the word calling he dissents from the common view: it must not be taken in the modern sense of a profession or condition in life, since it is nowhere so used in the New Testament but always signifies God’s calling of us, so that the charge is to continue to be Christians of the kind God’s call made you. He warns that those who count a ceremony unimportant often magnify the very disregard of it into a necessary virtue, against which the apostle guards by declaring both circumcision and uncircumcision nothing, and points to the circumcising of Timothy and the refusal to circumcise Titus as illustrations at once of the truth here enforced and of the apostle’s scrupulous adherence to his own principles. Barnes explains that the removal of the marks of circumcision was often attempted by men ashamed of having been circumcised, a practice which Jewish writers describe, and supposes that the very use of the English word calling for a profession arose from the belief that God calls every man to the rank he occupies, so that each has a call to his trade as really as a minister has to his; the keeping of the commandments, he adds, is the main thing and can be done whether a man is circumcised or not. Robertson says that the verse states the general principle which settles these questions and is afterwards illustrated by the cases of circumcision and slavery, so that while there is to be no compulsory bondage between the believer and the pagan there is to be no reckless abuse of the liberty either; the point of the illustration is that a Jew is to remain a Jew and a Gentile a Gentile, both standing on an equality in the churches, and this freedom about circumcision illustrates the freedom about Gentile mixed marriages. Lightfoot supplies a stranger fact from the rabbins, that some Jews always went uncircumcised, and that some priests who were not circumcised ministered at the altar without complaint and indeed without any fault, which the fathers of the traditions themselves confess.

debates: What the word calling means here: Ellicott insists that it never bears the modern sense of a profession or station in the New Testament but always means God’s call to us, so that the charge is to remain the kind of Christian that call made one, while Barnes derives the English usage from the belief that God calls each man to his rank, and Gill, Wesley and Calvin take it of the outward station and lawful mode of life

How the rule bears on what precedes: Ellicott makes it a limitation on the broad liberty of separation just granted, since the believer is never to cause or promote a parting, and Robertson takes it as the general principle governing all these questions, illustrated afterwards by circumcision and by slavery
outliers: Lightfoot reports from the rabbins that some Jews always went uncircumcised, and that uncircumcised priests ministered at the altar without complaint or fault
Clarke notes that the marks of circumcision could be removed by art and that Celsus himself prescribes the method
Ellicott sets the circumcising of Timothy beside the refusal to circumcise Titus as showing the apostle keeping his own rule in both directions

21.pericope_label: The slave and the freedman: Christ’s freedman, Christ’s bondservant, and abiding with God

schools.summary: Gill takes the opening of one called by grace while in the condition of a servant, understands the calling here not of any civil calling or office nor of the outward call by the ministry of the word only but of an internal, special and saving call out of darkness into light and out of bondage into liberty, and notes that the address as brethren is meant to engage them, since whatever the difference in their civil state there was none in their religious one. Calvin says the apostle’s whole object is to satisfy their consciences, exhorting servants to be of good cheer and not cast down as though servitude hindered them in serving God, and to be content in mind rather than concerned how to throw off the yoke; he infers that the difference of ranks and stations in the world is owing to the providence of God and that a regard to them is enjoined by his word. The paradox of the freedman and the bondservant he sees working in opposite directions, the one alleviating the bitterness of servitude for men who feel their situation mean and despicable, the other restraining the free-born lest they be unduly elated on account of a more honourable condition and lifted up with pride. The prohibition he narrows to obedience, since servants are to take heed not to subject themselves to the wicked or depraved inclinations of their masters, being holy to the Lord who redeemed them and not to defile themselves for the sake of men; and he guards the rule from the other side, that men are not bound here by a perpetual necessity so as never to change their condition if a fit occasion offers, the apostle simply repressing those thoughtless humours which hurry men hither and thither in a continual restlessness.

Clarke takes the permission that follows to mean that a man should prefer liberty for the sake of freedom and the temporal advantages connected with it, holds that a slave’s condition does not vitiate any of the privileges to which he is entitled as a Christian while free men who receive the grace of Christ must reckon themselves the slaves of the Lord and his real property, to be employed and disposed of according to his godly wisdom, and will find the service of that Master to be perfect freedom. He reports the interrogative rendering of the next verse, whether they have been bought out of their slavery, and the counsel drawn from it never to sell themselves again but to retain the liberty they have acquired; and he suspects that some of the Corinthian slaves had concluded that their Christian privileges absolved them from continuing slaves, or at least set them on a level with their Christian masters, a spirit which would soon have bred confusion and insubordination and brought scandals into the Church. Wesley bids the slave not anxiously seek liberty but embrace the opportunity if it comes, says that those who belong to God should not, where it can be avoided, become the bondslaves of men, which may expose them to many temptations, and reads the closing charge as doing all things unto God and in his immediate presence, so that those who abide with him preserve a holy indifference about outward things.

Barnes sets the scale of the question, since slaves abounded in Greece and in every part of the heathen world, Athens in her best days having twenty thousand freemen and four hundred thousand slaves, so that it was a very important matter to inquire what ought to be done; the paradox of the freedman he calls a delicate and happy argument designed to reconcile the slave to his condition, since the bondage he has been freed from was far more grievous than the one he is in, and the prohibition he makes a matter of self-regard, that even in that humble relation they are to think of themselves as serving God. Ellicott renders the opening as a question about the past, whether a man was called while a slave, and answers that the fact of being in slavery does not affect the reality or completeness of his conversion, so that he need feel no anxiety to escape from servitude; he renders the paradox as meaning that the man converted as a slave is Christ’s freedman while the man converted free is Christ’s slave, distinguishes a freedman from a freeman as one who has been in bondage and is now out of it, and turns the prohibition back on the argument of the chapter, that they are not to yield to other men’s views by seeking to change the condition of their calling. Robertson notes that slavery was usually a fixed condition and that a slave could be a good servant of Christ even under a heathen master, points out that there is no pronoun at all in the Greek of the permission and asks what is to be supplied, freedom or bondage, answering that freedom is the natural word, explains the term for freedman as an old word for a manumitted slave and adds that Christ paid the ransom of his own life so that he is the patron to whom the freedman owes everything, takes the prohibition at its widest as Paul’s clear opposition to human slavery as an institution, which comes out so powerfully in the letter to Philemon, and finds the comfort of the closing phrase in this, that even a slave can have God at his side by remaining at God’s side. Lightfoot asks whether the apostle speaks the words about not becoming servants of men as his own sense at all or puts them as an objection which he answers in the verse following, and recalls that the Jews were wont to object in just this way on the strength of the liberty they had obtained in the redemption out of Egypt, refusing to be called anything but free.

debates: What the permission use it rather refers to: Robertson points out that the Greek supplies no pronoun and asks whether freedom or bondage is to be understood, judging freedom the natural word, while Clarke and Wesley take the liberty for granted and bid a man embrace the opportunity, and Calvin turns the whole passage the other way, bidding servants be content in mind rather than concerned how to throw off the yoke

What the prohibition against becoming servants of men forbids: Robertson finds in it Paul’s settled opposition to slavery as an institution, Calvin restricts it to obeying the corrupt inclinations of masters, Barnes makes it a matter of how a Christian regards himself, Ellicott turns it against restlessness about one’s outward condition, and Lightfoot asks whether the words are the apostle’s own or an objection he is answering
outliers: Barnes gives the figures for Athens in her best days, twenty thousand freemen against four hundred thousand slaves
Robertson reads the verse as the settled position which comes out so powerfully in the letter to Philemon
Lightfoot recalls the rabbinic refusal to be called anything but free, on the strength of the redemption out of Egypt

25.pericope_label: Now concerning virgins: no command of the Lord, but a faithful judgment for the present distress

schools.summary: Gill takes the opening as one of the cases put to the apostle and written about by the Corinthians, whether virgins should continue in the same state or not, whether they should marry or not, and reads the answer that follows as the opinion of the apostle, the sentiment of his mind and his judgment in the case, that it was better and more advisable and eligible for persons that were single to continue so, with the reason for it following. Calvin says the apostle now returns to treat of marriage, of which he had begun to speak at the commencement of the chapter, stating more explicitly what he had previously touched upon briefly and somewhat obscurely, and speaking throughout conditionally because the matter is liable to be misapprehended and full of difficulties. He understands the term of virginity itself. On the disclaimer he says the Lord does not in any part of the Scriptures declare what persons ought to remain unmarried; on the contrary, inasmuch as the Scripture says that male and female were created together, it seems as if it called every one equally and without exception to marriage, and celibacy is nowhere enjoined upon any one or commended. The word Paul employs he takes from Beza as signifying not merely advice but a decisive judgment, an authoritative sentence, and he warns that the papists rashly infer from the verse that it is allowable to go beyond the limits of God’s word, since nothing was farther from Paul’s intention; the apostle advances nothing but what is included in what Christ says, and only anticipates the objection that he has no express precept in the law. He secures authority for the decision by declaring that he does not speak simply as a man but as a faithful teacher of the Church and an Apostle of Christ, and he ascribes that faithfulness to mercy. On the distress he differs from the Vulgate and Erasmus in the division of the words, following ancient and approved manuscripts which make it all one sentence rather than a repetition, and gives the sense that celibacy is expedient on account of the necessity with which the saints are always harassed in this life.

Henry says the apostle here resumes his discourse and gives directions to virgins how to act, and takes notice first of the manner in which he introduces them: there is no express and universal law delivered by the Lord himself concerning celibacy, but Paul gives his judgment as one who has obtained mercy of the Lord to be faithful, namely in the apostleship. He acted faithfully, and therefore his direction was to be regarded as a rule of Christ, for he gave judgment as a faithful apostle of Christ; though Christ had before delivered no universal law about the matter, he now gives direction by an inspired apostle. Henry draws the note that faithfulness in the ministry is owing to the grace and mercy of Christ, what Paul was ready to acknowledge upon all occasions, and that it is a great mercy which those obtain from God who prove faithful in the ministry of his word, whether ordinary or extraordinary. On the determination itself he holds that, considering the present distress, a state of celibacy was preferable, and that the wording is modest but delivered notwithstanding with apostolic authority: it is not the mere opinion of a private man but the very determination of the Spirit of God in an apostle, though thus spoken, and it was delivered in this way to give it the more weight, since those prejudiced against the apostle might have rejected the advice had it come with a merely authoritative air. Ministers, he adds, do not lose their authority by prudent condescensions, but must become all things to all men that they may do them the more good. The distress he explains historically: Christians at the first planting of their religion were grievously persecuted and continually liable to be tossed and hurried, so that the married state, bringing more care and cumber along with it, would make persecution more terrible and render them less able to bear it; whence he draws the rule that Christians in regulating their conduct should not barely consider what is lawful in itself but what is expedient in their circumstances.

Clarke says this was another subject on which the Church at Corinth had asked the advice of the apostle, and presses the sense of the word: we take it to signify a pure, unmarried young woman, but it is evident that in this place it means young unmarried persons of either sex, as appears from the verses that follow, and the word is frequently applied to men as well as to women. He cites Suidas under the entry for Abel, that he was a virgin and a righteous man, and notes that later in the chapter the word is supposed to mean the state of virginity or celibacy, with very probable reasons assigned for it. On the distress he observes that there was no period in the heathen times when the Church was not under persecutions and afflictions, though on some occasions these were more oppressive than at others, and defines the word as signifying necessity, distress, tribulation and calamity, comparing its use elsewhere in the New Testament. In such times, when the people of God had no certain dwelling-place and were lying at the mercy of their enemies without any protection from the state, the state itself often among the persecutors, he who had a family to care for would find himself in very embarrassed circumstances, since it would be much easier to provide for his personal safety alone. Wesley agrees with Clarke that the word covers either sex, and explains the disclaimer as meaning no particular revelation, adding that none was necessary, for the apostles wrote nothing which was not divinely inspired, but with this difference, that sometimes they had a particular revelation and a special commandment while at other times they wrote from the divine light which abode with them, the standing treasure of the Spirit of God; and this also was not their private opinion but a divine rule of faith and practice. He takes the mercy obtained as God having made him faithful in his apostolic office, so that he faithfully delivers what he receives. On the distress Wesley draws the inference more narrowly than the others: while any church is under persecution it is good for a man to continue as he is, whether married or unmarried, and St Paul does not here urge the present distress as a reason for celibacy any more than for marriage, but for a man’s not seeking to alter his state, whatever it be, but making the best of it.

Barnes calls this the third subject on which the opinion of Paul seems to have been asked by the church at Corinth, whether it was proper that those who had unmarried daughters or wards should give them in marriage, and suggests two reasons why the question may have been proposed: that in the existing state of persecution and trial it might be thought advisable to keep them from the additional cares of a family, and that some may already have been advocates for celibacy as more favourable to piety and altogether to be preferred. He notes that this opinion had an early prevalence and gave rise to the establishment of nunneries, an opinion everywhere attended with licentiousness and corruption, so that it was well the authority of an apostle should be employed to sanction and honour the marriage union. The judgment given he takes as opinion or advice from a Christian who has been pardoned and enlightened, one who would not advise for any selfish or mercenary or worldly consideration; the advice of such a devoted, self-denying, experienced man is entitled to respectful deference even where there is no claim to inspiration, and Paul had a special claim to give it because he was the founder of the church at Corinth. On the distress he takes the words of calamity and persecution then pressing, and adds the caution that Paul by no means meant this to be a permanent arrangement in the church, so that it cannot be urged as an argument for the monastic system. Ellicott introduces the passage as a new subject, the duty of parents regarding their young unmarried daughters, the answer to which occupies the rest of the section, and holds that the Apostle has no actual command from Christ because it was a point to which our Lord had not directly alluded; the contrast, he insists, is not between Paul inspired by the Lord and Paul not inspired, but between Paul quoting the words of Christ and Paul himself instructing as an inspired Apostle. He renders the next verse as because of the impending distress, that it is good for a person to continue in the state in which he is, married or unmarried, and finds the construction of the sentence strikingly characteristic of a writing taken down from dictation, since the speaker commences it and afterwards commences it over again. Robertson traces the word for commandment to a late formation and observes that Paul did have a command from the Lord at the earlier point, as we have it in Matthew and Mark; it was quite possible for him to know that command as he knew other sayings of Jesus even if he had as yet no access to a written gospel and no direct revelation, since sayings of Jesus were passed on among the believers, but on virgins he had no specific word. He limits the term to young unmarried women and not the metaphorical use in the Revelation, and takes the judgment as a deliberately formed decision from knowledge rather than a mere passing fancy, holding that the language about having obtained mercy, so far from being a disclaimer of inspiration, is an express claim to help from the Lord in forming a duly considered judgment which is in no sense a command but an inspired opinion. On the distress he parses the participle as standing on or present, compares its use elsewhere, and thinks Paul probably has in mind the hoped-for second coming and the calamities Jesus had said would precede it. Lightfoot sets out the two questions the Corinthians had asked by letter, concerning marriages between a believer and an unbeliever and concerning the marriages of virgins or single persons, and remarks that how a scruple should arise to them in the latter is somewhat obscure, since among the Jewish Christians a scruple might rather arise whether it were lawful for a single man to abstain from marriage at all.

debates: Whom the word virgins covers: Clarke and Wesley take it of young unmarried persons of either sex, citing Suidas on Abel, Robertson restricts it to young unmarried women, and Calvin takes the term as virginity itself

What the disclaimer concedes: Ellicott and Robertson hold that it distinguishes quoting Christ from teaching as an inspired apostle and claims rather than disclaims help from the Lord, Wesley distinguishes a particular revelation from the standing treasure of the Spirit, Calvin makes the word a decisive judgment and warns against the papist inference, and Henry calls it the very determination of the Spirit of God though modestly worded

How far the present distress carries: Barnes denies that it establishes any permanent arrangement or supports the monastic system, Wesley says it is urged no more for celibacy than for marriage but only against seeking to alter one’s state, and Robertson connects it with the expected coming of Christ
outliers: Clarke cites Suidas under the entry for Abel, that he was a virgin and a righteous man
Ellicott takes the doubled construction as evidence of dictation
Calvin follows ancient manuscripts in making the verse one proposition rather than a repetition, against Erasmus and the Vulgate
Lightfoot notes that the Jewish scruple would more naturally run the other way, whether abstaining from marriage was lawful at all

27.pericope_label: Bound or loosed: seek no change, yet whoever marries has not sinned

schools.summary: Gill takes the bond of a wife as constituted either by promise, by espousal or by consummate marriage, each of them a tie and an obligation and especially the last, and holds that marriage is such a bond as cannot be dissolved but by the death of one of the parties, unless in the case of adultery or of wilful desertion. He stresses that the bond obliges mutually: as the husband is bound by the law of marriage to live chastely and lovingly with his wife and to take care of her and provide for her, so the wife is bound by the same law to live in like manner with her husband and to submit unto him and obey him. On the concession he is emphatic that if a man who has never been married, or one who has been legally loosed from his wife, thinks fit to marry, he commits no sin and breaks no law of God, far from it, for marriage is honourable in all; the apostle would be understood as not dissuading from marriage as a thing sinful and criminal, but only as advising that it was more advisable for such as could to abstain under the present circumstances of things, and what he says of a man holds equally true of a virgin. Calvin makes the first clause a deliberate restriction upon the preceding commendation of celibacy, lest any one influenced by that praise should turn his thoughts to it and despise marriage, forgetful of his own necessity; and he finds in the words not merely a prohibition of breaking up the connection of marriage but a repression of the dislikes that are wont to creep in, that every one may continue to live with his wife willingly and cheerfully. The second clause he takes with a reservation manifest from the whole context, since the apostle does not allow to all the choice of perpetual celibacy but only to those to whom it is given, and he warns that no one who is not constrained by any necessity should rashly ensnare himself, for liberty ought not to be lightly thrown away or abandoned without much thought. On the concession he sees a scruple removed, since one might think from the preceding statement that he tempted God if he knowingly and willingly bound himself to marriage and so renounced his liberty; the emphatic word intimates that even where no positive necessity urges, the unmarried are not prohibited from marrying whenever they see fit, and beyond all controversy Paul designed to extend the liberty of marriage to all. Against those who read the mention of the virgin as an amplification, on the ground that loosing the virgin girdle approaches nearer to a fault than entering a second marriage after a husband’s death, he holds rather that the apostle makes virgins and widows simply equal in liberty of marriage; and he recalls that second marriages among the ancients were not without some mark of reproach, matrons who had contented themselves with one marriage being adorned with a chaplet of chastity, an honour that tended to reflect reproach upon those who had married repeatedly.

Clarke explains the first question as meaning simply married, since the marriage contract was considered in the light of a bond, and gives the counsel in two directions: neither regret your circumstances, notwithstanding the present distress, nor seek on that account for a dissolution of the marriage contract; but if you are under no matrimonial engagements, do not for the present enter into any. On the concession he says that there is no law against marrying even in the present distress, so that the man who marries has not sinned, and that it is only on account of prudential reasons that the advice is given at all. He insists that both the man and the woman have equal privileges in the case, either of them being free to marry without sin, and suspects a definite target, since as there were many sects and parties in Corinth it is probable that there were among them those who forbade to marry, as the apostle warns elsewhere, and who might have maintained other doctrines of devils besides; these persons, or such doctrines, he has in view when he says that they may marry and yet not sin. The trouble in the flesh Clarke traces to the simple circumstance of the incumbrance of a family while under persecution, because of the difficulty of providing for its comfort and safety while flying before the face of persecution; and he reads the closing words as meaning that the evil is coming, but the apostle will not press upon them the observance of a prudential caution which they might deem too heavy a cross. Wesley glosses the trouble as many outward troubles, and takes the sparing to mean that the apostle speaks as little and as tenderly as possible.

Barnes takes the first question as asking whether a man is already married, marriage being often represented as a tie or a bond, and the counsel as forbidding him to seek a dissolution of the connexion either by divorce or by separation. The second he insists is mistranslated: it should have been rendered free from a wife, or art thou single, and it does not imply of necessity that the person had ever been married, though it may bear that meaning and cover those who had been separated from a wife by her death; there is no necessity of supposing that Paul refers to persons who had divorced their wives, and he cites Grotius, Schleusner and Doddridge as agreeing. On the concession he says there is no express command of God on the subject, the counsel given being mere advice which may be observed or not as they shall judge best, since marriage is honourable and lawful and no law prohibits it though circumstances may make it inadvisable. He extends the principle to other cases: the same advice would be proper in a time of persecution, or where a man is poor and cannot support a family, or where he has already a dependent mother and sisters to be supported by him, or where the cares of a family would take up the time and efforts he might otherwise give to a missionary life, so that he may be free from these cares and give himself with more undivided interest to the salvation of men. The trouble in the flesh he expounds as anxiety, care, solicitude and trials, with days of persecution coming on in which families might be torn asunder and members put to death, or the household driven from home into exile for religion; and the closing words he reads as a refusal to dwell on a melancholy theme and pain their hearts by describing it. Ellicott calls the first verse an explanation and re-assertion of the previous words, and holds that being loosed from a wife does not mean a separation after marriage but simply unmarried. In the concession he prefers the past tense throughout, if however thou hast married, and holds that the teaching is not for some who will persist in marrying after this advice but still refers to those actually married, with a further and clearer statement to them that the question is not one of sin but merely of desirability; noting that the original is emphatically if the virgin have married, he suggests that in the letter from Corinth some particular case was referred to in which a Christian parent had scruples about allowing his daughter to marry, and that while dealing with the subject generally the Apostle refers immediately to the case which gave rise to the inquiry. The troubles he glosses as earthly troubles, not a spiritual question at all, and the closing words he takes not as a refusal to harass them with detail but as a statement of the apostle’s whole motive: matrimony will involve you in earthly troubles when the expected distress comes, and therefore in advising you to remain unmarried my desire is to spare you them. Robertson parses the perfect passive of the binding and the present imperative of the prohibition, do not be seeking release, notes that the word for release occurs here only in the New Testament, and includes bachelors as well as widowers under the participle for the loosed. He observes that Paul urges this advice only because of the present necessity, that we do not know whether he held to the opinion later, that he certainly gives the noblest view of marriage in the letter to the Ephesians, and that he does not present this as his opinion for all men at all times, since men feel it their duty to seek a wife. In the concession he analyses the third-class condition with the ingressive aorist subjunctive and explains the aorist of the apodosis either as timeless and gnomic or as a swift proleptic transition from the future to the past, such mixed conditions being common, and notes that the same construction recurs for the virgin with only an older form of the subjunctive, the manuscripts interchanging both examples with no special point in the difference. He marks the emphatic position of the word for tribulation, comparing the thorn in the flesh, and suggests that the closing verb may be conative, I am trying to spare you.

debates: What being loosed from a wife means: Barnes argues from Grotius, Schleusner and Doddridge that it means simply unmarried and need not imply a previous marriage at all, Ellicott agrees that it is not a separation after marriage, and Robertson brings bachelors as well as widowers under the term, against any reading that would make the verse concern divorced men

What the apostle means by sparing them: Ellicott takes it as the motive of the whole advice, that remaining unmarried will spare them the coming troubles, while Barnes, Clarke and Wesley take it of the manner of speaking, that he will not dwell on a melancholy theme or press a caution they might feel too heavy, and Robertson allows a conative sense, I am trying to spare you

Whether the mention of the virgin amplifies the case of the widow: Calvin reports the view that loosing the virgin girdle was nearer a fault than a second marriage, so that the argument would run from the harder case to the easier, but judges instead that the apostle simply makes the two equal in liberty
outliers: Calvin recalls the chaplet of chastity given to matrons content with a single marriage, and the honorific formula of ancient inscriptions
Clarke reads the concession as aimed at Corinthian parties who forbade to marry
Barnes applies the counsel to poverty, dependent relatives and the claims of missionary labour
Robertson sets the passage against the account of marriage in the letter to the Ephesians

29.pericope_label: The time is shortened: having, weeping, rejoicing and buying as though not, for the fashion of this world passes away

schools.summary: Gill offers two readings of the shortened time and does not choose between them. Either the time of life is very short and it is but a little while to the end of the world and the second coming of Christ, so that since the marriage state is full of care and affords less time for the service of Christ, it is most advisable to continue in a single life and be more at leisure to use that little time for spiritual good, the edification of others and the glory of Christ; or the apostle is still enlarging upon the former argument taken from the present time being one of distress and persecution, in which case the phrase means the time is contracted and full of anguish and affliction, and is the same thing as the present necessity and the trouble in the flesh already mentioned. On the weeping he is careful to deny that the apostle here introduces and establishes a stoical apathy, or would have persons show no manner of concern at troubles and crosses, at things adverse and afflicting in a marriage state, or at the loss of wives or children; he directs rather to a moderate use of sorrow, to such a degree as not to hinder and divert from the exercises of piety and religion. On the use of the world he takes it of those who have a large affluence of the things of this world, who should use them in a moderate and temperate manner and not squander them away extravagantly or spend them on their lusts and use them intemperately, which is to abuse them. Calvin reads the passage as a discourse on the holy use of marriage, aimed at repressing the wantonness of those who, when they have married, think of nothing but the delights of the flesh and have no remembrance of God; he exhorts believers not to give way to unbridled desire in such a way that marriage should have the effect of plunging them into the world, since marriage is a remedy for incontinency and has that effect if it be used with moderation, married persons living together chastely in the fear of the Lord and using marriage like the other helps of this earthly life with their hearts directed upwards to meditation on the heavenly life. His argument he draws from the shortness of human life, which is frail and of short duration, so that we should not be held entangled by it, and he remarks that every one has this philosophy in his mouth but few have it truly and in good earnest impressed upon their minds. On the compound verb he observes that the preposition in composition is generally taken in a bad sense or at least denotes intensity, so that the word here means abusing or using too much, and that the term is frequently used by classical writers in this sense; Paul therefore directs us to a sober and frugal use of things, such as may not impede or retard our course but may allow of our always hastening forward toward the goal. In the word for fashion he finds the vanity of the world elegantly expressed, there being nothing firm or solid in this world but a mere show or outward appearance, and he suspects an allusion to theatrical representations, in which on the curtain being drawn up in a single moment a new appearance is presented and the things that held the eyes of the spectators in astonishment are immediately gone.

Clarke reads the shortened time strictly of the coming persecutions and of the brevity of life: these persecutions and distresses are at the door and life itself will soon be run out, and even then Nero was plotting those grievous persecutions with which he not only afflicted but devastated the Church of Christ. He therefore bids none begin to think of any comfortable settlement for his family, but sit loose to all earthly concerns and stand ready prepared to escape for his life or meet death as the providence of God may permit, since the husband will be dragged from the side of his wife to appear before the magistrates and be required either to abjure Christ or die; and he quotes the ode of Horace on the earth and the house and the pleasing consort that must be left, of which none but the hated cypress will follow its short-lived lord, adding that poor heathenism could give but cold comfort in such circumstances as these. On the weeping and rejoicing he foresees a system of distress and confusion so complete that private sorrows and private joys will be absorbed in weightier and more oppressive public evils, yet every man is still to continue in his calling and to buy and sell and traffic as usual, though in a short time either by the coming persecution or by the levelling hand of death he who had earthly property will be brought into the same circumstances as he who had none. On the use of the world he bids those who have earthly property or employments discharge their duties conscientiously from a conviction of the instability of earthly things, making a right use of everything and perverting nothing from its use, since to use a thing is to employ it properly to accomplish the end to which it refers and to abuse it is to pervert it from that use; and he suspects that the word for world here is taken in its frequent sense of the Jewish state and polity, whose destruction was then at hand, which the Holy Spirit might then be signifying to the apostle. Wesley takes the announcement as made with great confidence, that the time of our abode here is short, and draws the plain consequence that even those who have wives should be as serious, zealous, active, dead to the world, as devoted to God and as holy in all manner of conversation as if they had none, marking how easy the transition is by which the apostle slides from everything else to the one thing needful and, forgetting whatever is temporal, is swallowed up in eternity.
