Each of the remaining clauses he glosses in a phrase: sorrowful yet always rejoicing, joy tempered with godly fear, buyers who know themselves to be only stewards and not proprietors, and the use of the world as not seeking happiness in it but in God, using everything therein only in such a manner and degree as most tends to the knowledge and love of God. The fashion of this world he expounds as the whole scheme of things, this marrying and weeping and rejoicing and all the rest, which not only will pass but now passeth away and is this moment flying off like a shadow.

Barnes takes the opening as a reminder that whatever a man’s condition or rank in life, it matters little if he is ready to depart to a better world, and explains the word for shortened as one commonly applied to the act of furling a sail, reducing it into a narrow compass, and then to anything reduced within narrow limits. He allows that there may be a reference to the time being contracted by their impending persecutions and trials, but insists that it is always equally true that time is short and will soon glide away, so that the plans of life should all be formed in view of this truth and no plan adopted which does not contemplate it. On the weeping he concedes that it is impossible for human nature not to feel when persecuted, maligned or slandered, or when near earthly friends are taken away, but holds that religion will calm the troubled spirit, pour oil on the agitated waves, light up a smile in the midst of tears and produce joy even in the midst of sorrow, keeping us from immoderate grief while nature still forces the tear of mourning, since Christ sweat great drops of blood and Christians often weep, yet the heart may be calm and confident in God in the severest tempest of calamity. On the use of the world he distinguishes the lawful use, which furnishes raiment, food, clothing, medicine and protection and for which the world was made, from the compound which he takes as using too much and too freely, not merely intensive but denoting evil, so that we are not to give our appetites to indulgence or our days and nights to revelry. The word for fashion he takes as the form or appearance, probably drawn from the shifting scenes of the drama, where when the scene changes the imposing and splendid pageantry passes off. Ellicott denies that the opening reiterates what has been said and calls it a solemn and affectionate warning, urging that whether or not they applied the principle to marriage it is true and of vast importance in regulating all life, that men should live ever expecting the return of the Lord; and he refuses to let this principle be thought a deduction from a mistaken belief that the Second Advent was close at hand, since it was taught by Christ himself, who warned men against living carelessly because they thought the Lord delayed his coming and bade them be ever on the watch, as servants for the unexpected return of their master and as guests for the coming of the bridegroom. On the compound verb he says we can scarcely find a better English word than abusing, but that the word implies in modern language an abuse arising from misuse and not, as in the original, an abuse arising from over-much use; all the things mentioned in the series are right things, and the warning is against being in bondage to what is in itself right and good rather than against any criminal use of it. The fashion he renders as the outward form of this world which is passing away, and finds in it not a merely general reference to the ephemeral nature of things temporal but the Apostle’s conviction that the last days were already commencing and the outward temporal form of things being superseded. Robertson notes the change of verb in the introductory phrase and calls it a new turn given to the argument about the present necessity, parses the perfect periphrastic passive of the shortening, finds the verb in the papyri for curtailing expenses, and reports that Calvin takes it of the shortness of human life while judging that Paul rather pictures the foreshortening of time and opportunity because of the possible nearness of and hope for the second coming, though in Philippians he faces death as his fate while still looking for the coming. He explains the construction of the assumed condition with the participle as regular, takes the verb of possessing as holding fast, and says Paul means that all earthly relations are to hang loosely about us in view of the second coming. On the last pair he notes the accusative with the verb for using as a late resumption of the original construction, takes the compound as perfective, to use up or to use to the full, and prefers that to the sense of abusing, citing the papyri; and the verb of passing he renders as passing along like a moving panorama, the word used of Jesus passing by in Jericho.

debates: Whether the shortened time means the brevity of human life or the nearness of the end: Calvin takes it of life and Clarke of the imminent persecutions, Robertson reports Calvin’s view but judges that Paul pictures the foreshortening of opportunity before the second coming, Barnes allows the reference to their trials while insisting the truth is always equally true, and Gill sets out both readings without deciding

Whether the principle of living as expecting the Lord rests on a mistaken expectation: Ellicott argues at length that it does not, since Christ taught it himself and warned against presuming on delay, and that the conviction of nearness followed from the principle rather than producing it

What the compound rendered abusing means: Calvin, Ellicott and Robertson take it of excessive rather than criminal use, using too much or using up, while Barnes gives it a moral edge as denoting evil, and Clarke defines abuse as perverting a thing from its proper use
outliers: Clarke quotes Horace on the house, the lands and the pleasing consort that must be left, with only the hated cypress following its short-lived lord
Barnes explains the shortening from the furling of a sail
Calvin and Barnes both take the passing fashion from the stage, the drawn curtain and the changed scene, while Robertson makes it a moving panorama
Clarke suspects that the world whose fashion passes is the Jewish state and polity

32.pericope_label: Free from cares: the divided heart of the married, and a rule laid down without a snare

schools.summary: Gill takes the wish for freedom from care as another reason confirming the advice to virgins to remain such, since the married state is full of cares while the single life is more free of them; he wishes them to continue in such a state that they may be without the anxious and distracting cares of temporal things, things relating to the good decorum and sustenance of a family, and so be more free and at leisure for the service of God. The married man he describes as attending diligently to the business and calling of life he is engaged in, that he may provide food and clothing and other necessaries for the support of his family. On the difference between the wife and the virgin he reports the textual question, that the word rendered there is difference stands in some copies at the end of the previous verse, where the Vulgate Latin and Ethiopic versions render it and is divided, referring to the married man whose thoughts are distracted with the cares of the world and whose mind is divided between the Lord and his wife, between the things that please the one and those that please the other, so that he cannot attend upon the Lord without distraction as the unmarried person may; but he follows the more generally received reading, in which the apostle shows that there is just the same difference between a married and an unmarried woman as between a married and an unmarried man, no difference in nature or sex but in state and condition and in the cares which involve the one and the other. On the closing verse he insists that in giving the advice to abide single the apostle had nothing in view but their temporal and spiritual advantage, that they might be better able to grapple with persecution for the sake of the Gospel and be more at liberty to serve the Lord, and not that marriage is unlawful or the single life a more honest and chaste way of living or an incumbent duty; all that he had said was by way of advice, having faithfully laid before them the advantages and disadvantages of both states and left them at full liberty. Calvin says the apostle returns to the virgins he had spoken of but not yet fully explained, and at the outset pronounces as usual a commendation upon celibacy before allowing every one the liberty of choosing what suits him best; it is not without good reason that he returns so frequently to proclaim its advantages, for he saw that the burdens of matrimony were far from light, and the man who can exempt himself from them ought not to refuse such a benefit, while it is of advantage for those who resolve to marry to be forewarned of these inconveniences, so that they may not afterwards give way to despondency on meeting them unexpectedly, as happens to many who promise themselves unmixed honey and, disappointed in that expectation, are very readily cast down by the slightest mishap. On the married man’s care for the things of the world he explains that the world here means the condition of this earthly life, and refuses the inference that all who are married are therefore strangers to the kingdom of God as thinking of nothing but this earth: the Apostle speaks only of a portion of the thoughts, as though he had said that they have one eye directed to the Lord but in such a way as to have the other directed to their wife, marriage being like a burden by which the mind of a pious man is weighed down so that he does not move Godward with so much alacrity. He insists that these evils do not belong to marriage but proceed from the depravity of men, and rejects the calumnies of Jerome, who scrapes together all these things for the purpose of bringing marriages into disrepute. Of the women he says that virgins and widows are not prevented by earthly things from devoting their whole cares and affections to God, not that all act this part but that there is opportunity for it if the mind is so disposed; holiness in body and spirit shows what kind of chastity is true and acceptable to God, when the mind is kept unpolluted in his sight, and he wishes this were more carefully attended to, turning sharply on the devotement to the Lord commonly found among monks and nuns and the whole scum of the Papistical clergy, than whose celibacy nothing more obscene can be imagined. On the last verse he commends the Apostle’s moderation: though he knew the vexations and difficulties of married life and the advantages of celibacy, he does not venture to prescribe, but having commended celibacy and fearing that some readers might be led away by such commendations and say within themselves what the disciples said in reply to Christ, without taking their ability into view, he declares in express terms that he points out what is most advantageous but does not wish to impose a necessity upon any one.

Clarke turns the exhortation to freedom from care into counsel about providence: though all these things will shortly come to pass, do not be anxious about them, since every occurrence is under the direction and management of God, the wrath of man shall praise him and the remainder of it he shall restrain, and none can harm you if you be followers of that which is good; and he quotes the lines of Byrom advising us to run our course of duty with a patient mind, since God does nothing, nor suffers anything to be done, but what we would do ourselves could we see the end of all events as well as He. The unmarried man, he says, has nothing to do with a family and can therefore give his whole time to the service of his Maker, having him alone to please, while the married man has a family to provide for and his wife to please as well as to fulfil his duty to God and attend to the concerns of his own soul. On the comparison he is emphatic and generous to the married state: the single man has very little trouble comparatively and the married man a great deal; the single man is an atom in society while the married man is a small community in himself; the former is the centre of his own existence and lives for himself alone, while the latter is diffused abroad, makes a much more important part of the body social and provides both for its support and continuance; the single man lives for and does good to himself only, but the married man lives both for himself and the public, and both the state and the Church of Christ are dependent on him. Of the women he says the unmarried cares only for the things of the Lord, having no domestic duties to perform, and is separated to divine employments in body and spirit, whereas the married cares also for the things of the world and how she may please her husband, having many domestic duties to fulfil since her husband is obliged to leave to her the care of the family; and he reports that on this verse there is such a profusion of various readings in manuscripts, versions and fathers that he must refer the reader to Griesbach. On the closing verse he holds that the advices belong to the Corinthians alone because of the peculiar circumstances in which they were placed, nothing spoken here being designed for general application but only for that Church or Churches in similar circumstances; and in the word for snare he finds a manifest allusion to the Retiarius among the Romans, who carried a small casting net which he endeavoured to throw over the head of his adversary to entangle him, or to a similar Persian custom using a noose called the camand, one of which lies before him, a strong silken cord with a loop at one end to be held in the hand and the rest in the form of a noose which tightens in proportion as it is pulled. Wesley takes the freedom from care as freedom from any incumbrance of the thoughts, and qualifies each of the apostle’s statements with a condition: the unmarried man cares only for the things of the Lord if he understand and use the advantage he enjoys, and the unmarried woman if she know and use her privilege, all her time and care and thoughts centring in how she may be holy both in body and spirit, which he calls the standing advantage of a single life in all ages and nations, asking who makes a suitable use of it. The married, he allows, cares for the things of the world, and it is his duty so to do so far as becomes a Christian, providing all things needful for his wife and family. On the last verse he distinguishes those who are not able to receive this saying, on whom no snare is to be cast, from those who are able and for whose profit it is spoken, and explains the word rendered wait as signifying sitting close by a person in a good posture to hear, as Mary sat at the feet of Jesus, with the mind not drawn any way from its centre by any person or thing or care or incumbrance whatsoever.

Barnes explains the wish as regulating the whole advice, and glosses freedom from care as freedom from anxiety and solicitude, from such necessary attention to the things of this life as would take the thoughts and affections off heavenly objects. The unmarried man, he says, is not distracted by the cares of this life, his time is not engrossed and his affections not alienated by attendance on the concerns of a family, especially in times of trial and persecution, so that he can give his chief thoughts to the advancement of the Redeemer’s kingdom, as Paul’s own example showed. Of the married man he says he is under a necessity of giving attention to the things of the world and cannot give his undivided interest to religion, and he is plain about the danger the apostle intimates, that a man may be so anxious to gratify his wife as to interfere with his religious duties: the affections may be taken off the Lord and bestowed on her until she takes the place of God, or the time that should be given to secret prayer and the duties of religion may be consumed in devotion to her, or she may demand his company when he ought to be otherwise engaged. On the difference between the wife and the virgin he notes that the Greek word may mean is divided, giving the sense that the wife and the virgin are divided in the same manner, that is, that the same difference holds in their case as between the married and the unmarried man; the unmarried woman has more advantages for attending to the things of religion and fewer temptations to neglect her duty to God, and he suggests that the body is mentioned in her case, where it was not in the man’s, because her temptation would lie principally there. On the last verse he says the profit intended is that they may avail themselves of all their advantages and pursue the course that will most advance their piety and salvation, and takes the word for snare as meaning a cord, a rope or a bond, so that Paul would not bind them by any rule which God had not made nor restrain them from what is lawful; the same idea is usually conveyed by the word yoke and sometimes by the word burden. Ellicott takes the opening words as resuming the form of expression used earlier, I would spare you trouble and I also wish to have you free from anxious care, and says the Apostle here returns to the subject immediately under consideration and shows how what he has been saying bears upon it, since this element of anxious care must be borne in mind in considering the desirability of marriage. He notes important variations in the readings of these verses in the Greek manuscripts and sets out the emendations he thinks required in the text from which the Authorised version was translated, removing the full stop and inserting connectives so that the widow and the virgin are grouped together. On the last verse he explains that the instructions are given not to please the writer but emphatically for their own advantage, not to entangle them in a noose and so take away their liberty, but with a view to comeliness or honesty and to their waiting upon the Lord without being cumbered with earthly things, as Martha was cumbered. Robertson notes the old compound adjective for freedom from cares, found in the New Testament only here and in Matthew, and warns that care for the things of the Lord is the ideal state, since even the unmarried do let the cares of the world choke the word; he marks the deliberative subjunctive retained in the indirect question and the parallel constructions for pleasing the wife and pleasing the husband. On the difference between the wife and the virgin he calls the text very uncertain and almost hopelessly so, reports that Westcott and Hort put the verb in the previous verse and begin a new sentence adding the word for unmarried, so that the widow and the virgin are each anxious for the things of the Lord like the unmarried man, allows that this may be so but observes that the manuscripts vary greatly at every point, and holds that at any rate Paul’s point is that the married woman is more disposed to care for the things of the world, adding that many unmarried women are after the things of the world today and lead a fast and giddy life. On the last verse he parses the old adjective for advantageous and the reflexive plural, explains the word for snare as a noose or slip-knot used for lassoing animals with a papyrus example of a man hanged by a noose, and says Paul does not wish to capture the Corinthians by lasso and compel them to do what they do not wish about getting married; the aim he renders as decorum, from a word meaning shapely or comely, and the closing term as a late adjective meaning sitting well beside, for the good position beside the Lord.

debates: How the text of the clause distinguishing the wife and the virgin should read: Gill reports the variant that places the verb at the end of the previous verse, where the Vulgate and Ethiopic take it of the married man’s divided mind, Robertson calls the text almost hopelessly uncertain and gives the arrangement of Westcott and Hort grouping the widow with the virgin, Ellicott proposes his own emendations of the received text, and Clarke declines the question altogether and refers the reader to Griesbach

Whether the married state is a disadvantage: Calvin holds that the evils do not belong to marriage but proceed from the depravity of men and rejects Jerome’s use of the passage, Barnes sets out in detail the ways a wife may draw a man from his religious duties, and Clarke turns the comparison to the married man’s credit, as one who lives for the public and on whom both state and Church depend

How far the counsel binds: Clarke restricts it to the Corinthians and Churches in like circumstances, Calvin says the apostle points out what is most advantageous without imposing necessity, Wesley distinguishes those able to receive the saying from those not able, and Gill insists the whole was advice and left them at full liberty
outliers: Clarke finds the snare in the casting net of the Roman Retiarius, and in the Persian camand, one of which he has before him as he writes
Clarke quotes Byrom on running one’s course of duty with a patient mind
Calvin turns the verse on the celibacy of monks and nuns, and Robertson on unmarried women who lead a fast and giddy life
Wesley and Ellicott both read the closing words through the house at Bethany, Mary sitting at the feet of Jesus and Martha cumbered

36.pericope_label: The father and his virgin: giving in marriage does well, keeping her unmarried does better

schools.summary: Gill reports two ways of taking the person addressed: some understand a man engaged or betrothed to a virgin who protracts the marriage, and who may use his prudence in consummating it if he pleases for anything the apostle has said to the contrary, but he judges it better to understand a parent, or one who has the care and guardianship of virgins. On the steadfast heart he says the apostle returns to confirm his former advice where it can be safely attended to, observing that notwithstanding what he had allowed to be lawful and proper, a man who has deliberated upon and well weighed the matter of virginity and the case of a single life, and is at a point about it with no hesitation nor fluctuation of mind, and has also no necessity of acting otherwise either through the meanness of his circumstances or through the weakness of his virgin, she not having the gift of continency, does well to abide by his purpose. On the summary he says that he who gives her in marriage does that which is in its own nature good, agreeable to the will of God, of his institution and appointment, and answering many good ends and purposes; such a one, seeing a necessity for it and a propriety in it, does a very good thing, securing her chastity and his own credit, preventing fornication and other evils that might follow, and consulting the good of mankind and the honour of religion. Calvin says the apostle now directs his discourse to parents who had children under their authority, for having heard the praises of celibacy and the inconveniences of matrimony they might doubt whether it were at all a kind thing to involve their children in so many miseries, lest they should seem to blame for the troubles that might befall them; the greater their attachment to their children, the more anxiously they exercise fear and caution on their account. To relieve them of this difficulty Paul teaches that it is their duty to consult their children’s advantage exactly as one would do for himself when at his own disposal. On the steadfast purpose he is careful to distinguish it from the resolution formed by monks, a voluntary binding over to perpetual servitude such as their vow is; the apostle expressly mentions a settled purpose because mankind often contrive schemes which they regret the next day, and since the matter is of importance he requires a thoroughly matured purpose. He notes further that many, when about to deliberate, bring obstinacy with them rather than reason, and do not consider when they renounce marriage what is in their power but reckon it enough to say that such is their will. On the conclusion he says parents are free from blame if they give their daughters in marriage and do better if they keep them at home unmarried, but that celibacy is not preferred to marriage except under the exception already expressed: if the power to abstain be wanting on the daughter’s part, the father acts an exceedingly bad part in endeavouring to keep her back from marriage, and would be no longer a father to her but a cruel tyrant. The sum of the whole discussion he gives thus, that celibacy is better than marriage because it has more liberty, so that persons can serve God with greater freedom, but that no necessity ought to be imposed so as to make it unlawful for individuals to marry if they think proper, and further that marriage itself is a remedy granted by God to those who need it.

Henry takes the apostle here to be giving advice about the disposal of children in marriage upon the principle of his former determination, and supplies the social fact that makes the case intelligible: in that age and those parts of the world, and especially among the Jews, it was reckoned a disgrace for a woman to remain unmarried past a certain number of years, since it gave a suspicion of something that was not for her reputation. On that footing he paraphrases the whole passage. If any man thinks he behaves unhandsomely towards his daughter, and that it is not for her credit to remain unmarried when she is of full age, and that upon this principle it is needful to dispose of her in marriage, he may use his pleasure, and it is no sin in him to dispose of her to a suitable mate. But if a man has determined in himself to keep her a virgin, and stands to this determination, and is under no necessity to dispose of her in marriage but is at liberty, with her consent, to pursue his purpose, he does well in keeping her a virgin. In short, he who gives her in marriage does well, but he who keeps her single, where she is content to remain so, does better. Henry ties the whole judgment back to the circumstances of the time, the persecution and distress under which the church then lay, and treats the preference for the single state as resting on that footing rather than on any superior holiness belonging to celibacy in itself.

Clarke sets out three principal meanings that have been assigned to the verse. The first is that in those early times, both among the Hebrews and Christians, daughters were wholly in the power of the father, so that he might give or not give them in marriage as he chose and might bind them to perpetual celibacy if he thought proper; if such a father had devoted his daughter to perpetual virginity and afterwards found that she had fixed her affections upon a person whom she was strongly inclined to marry, and was now getting past the prime of life, then seeing from her circumstances that it would be wrong to force her to continue in celibacy he might alter his purpose without sin and let her and her suitor marry. The second is that the whole verse and its context speaks of young women dedicated to the service of God, who were called virgins in the primitive Church, and that a case is put in which circumstances might occur to render the breach of even a vow of this kind necessary, so that no sin would be committed. The third, which he reports as the opinion of both Locke and Whitby, is that the word does not mean a virgin at all but the state of virginity or celibacy, whether in a man or a woman. Whitby reasons that though it is generally supposed these three verses relate to virgins under the power of parents and guardians, and the usual inference drawn that children are to be disposed of in marriage by their parents, this may be true but has no foundation in the text, since the phrase is not to keep his daughter’s virginity but his own, or rather his own purpose of virginity; and Clarke cites Phavorinus, that he is called a virgin who freely gives himself up to the Lord, renouncing matrimony and preferring a life spent in continency. This must be the true import, Whitby argues, because the whole matter depends on the purpose of the man’s own heart, on the power he has over his own will, and on there being no necessity arising from himself to change that purpose, whereas the keeping of a daughter unmarried depends on none of these conditions on the father’s part but on her own: let her have a necessity, and the apostle would surely not advise the father to keep her a virgin because he had determined so to do, nor could there be any doubt whether the father had power over his own will when no necessity lay upon him to betroth his virgin. Wesley reads the verse simply of a parent who thinks he should otherwise act indecently, unbecoming his character, toward his virgin daughter if she be above age and need so require, in which case her suitor and she may marry; on the steadfast heart he glosses the absence of necessity as meaning where there is no such need, and the power over one’s own will as that which would otherwise incline a man to desire the increase of his family and its strengthening by new relations; and on the conclusion he adds only that the man does better if there be no necessity.

Barnes explains the uncomely behaviour as acting an unbecoming part, imposing an unnecessary, painful and improper constraint and crossing inclinations which are in themselves proper, and takes the virgin as the man’s daughter or ward or any unmarried female committed to his care. Passing the flower of her age he takes as passing the marriageable age and remaining unmarried, and notes that in the east it was regarded as peculiarly dishonourable to remain unmarried, so that the authority of a father might be the means of involving his daughter in shame and disgrace; where that would be the case it would be wrong to prohibit her marriage, and she ought to be allowed to marry if it would promote her happiness. The authority in the case he grants to the father, since in the east it resided there, and holds that he errs not whichever course he takes though in such a case marriage is advisable. On the steadfast heart he says most commentators understand it of the father and of his purpose of keeping his daughter from the marriage connexion, and opposes standing steadfast to a disposition that is vacillating and unsettled, denoting a man who has command of himself and adheres to his purpose and to whose happiness and reputation it is important that he should not be thought easily moved; the absence of necessity he takes as meaning that there is nothing in her disposition or inclination that would make marriage necessary and no engagement or obligation that would be violated, and the power over his own will as freedom from being bound in the case by another. The conclusion he glosses briefly, that the one does right and violates no law and is not to be blamed, while the other does what is on the whole to be preferred if it can be done, more certainly consulting her happiness in the present circumstances. Ellicott says the writer here turns to the duty of parents, with a further explanation that the previous expressions are not binding commandments but apostolic advice, and takes the unfair behaviour as exposing the daughter to temptation by withholding permission for her marriage. He denies that the permission means the father may consent or not and be right either way, since it is implied in the earlier part of the sentence that he thinks he ought to give his consent and therefore wishes to; let him do what he so wills, says the Apostle, and he need not fear that he does wrong. The steadfast verse he holds must be limited strictly to cases where positive harm is likely to result from the parent withholding consent, the contrast being between the parent whose will must be under the control of external necessity and the parent who has power over his own will and has made his resolution in his heart. On the conclusion he makes a fine point of the tenses, the present for the man who gives his daughter in marriage as if the good he did began and ended there, and the future for the man who does not, the good result of his action continuing while the girl remains with her parent; the passage clearly shows, he says, that the Apostle has not been contrasting right and wrong but comparative degrees of what is expedient, and throughout he takes for granted the absolute control of the parent over the child in accordance with the principles of both Greek and Jewish jurisprudence, so that no advice is given to the young maiden herself but only to her father. Robertson parses the old verb for behaving unseemly and the compound adjective for being past the bloom of youth, both occurring only here in the New Testament, and supposes that the Corinthians had asked Paul about the duty of a father towards a daughter old enough to marry; Paul has discussed the problem on the grounds of expediency and now faces the question where the daughter wishes to marry and there is no serious objection, and the father is advised to consent, Roman and Greek fathers having control of the marriage of their daughters, as the line of Hermione in Euripides shows, that her marriage is her father’s care and not for her to decide. The steadfast verse he takes of the case where the virgin daughter does not wish to marry and the father agrees with her. On the conclusion he notes that the verb for giving in marriage has not been found outside the New Testament, refers the preference to the present distress and the shortened time, and adds that when all is said Paul leaves the whole problem of getting married an open question to be settled by each individual case.

debates: Whose virginity is in question: Clarke reports the view of Locke and Whitby that the word means the state of celibacy and that what is kept is the man’s own purpose of virginity, arguing that the conditions named fit only him and not a daughter, against the common view of Gill, Henry, Barnes, Ellicott, Robertson and Calvin that a father is disposing of a daughter; Clarke also records a second reading that refers the passage to women vowed to the service of God in the primitive Church, and Gill notes the further alternative of a betrothed man delaying his own marriage

What the steadfast purpose excludes: Calvin distinguishes it sharply from the monastic vow and requires a thoroughly matured resolution rather than obstinacy, while Barnes opposes it to a vacillating temper and Ellicott confines the preceding permission to cases of positive harm

How far the preference for keeping her unmarried reaches: Ellicott holds that the passage compares degrees of expediency and not right and wrong, Calvin allows the preference only where the daughter has the power to abstain and calls the father a cruel tyrant otherwise, and Robertson refers it to the present distress and leaves the question open to each case
outliers: Robertson quotes Hermione in Euripides, that her marriage is her father’s care and not hers to decide
Clarke cites Phavorinus on the man who freely gives himself up to the Lord, renouncing matrimony
Henry and Barnes both explain the case from the reproach attaching to an unmarried woman in that age
Ellicott builds an argument on the change from the present tense to the future between the two halves of the conclusion

39.pericope_label: The widow at liberty, only in the Lord: happier if she so abide, and I think I have the Spirit of God

schools.summary: Gill takes the opening as meaning that the wife is bound to her husband by the law of marriage during his life, and that the bond of marriage between them cannot be dissolved but by the death of one of them, except in the cases of adultery and of wilful desertion. On the closing preference he explains that the happiness spoken of is not the happiness of another world but of this: the apostle’s meaning is that a widow in an unmarried state would be more free from cares and less liable to trouble, would live with more peace and quietness and be more at leisure to serve the Lord, second marriages oftentimes proving more disagreeable than the first; and in this the apostle only gives his opinion, enjoining nothing by way of command or in an authoritative manner. Calvin explains why women needed a separate word at all: the apostle had previously spoken indiscriminately of husbands and wives, but since wives, on account of the modesty of their sex, might seem to have less liberty, he thought it necessary to give some special directions with reference to them, and now teaches that women are not less at liberty than men to marry a second time on becoming widows. He then turns the point into a protest against a long-standing prejudice. Those who desired a second marriage were branded with the reproach of intemperance, and with a view to putting some slight upon them those who had been contented with being once married were wont to be presented with the chaplet of chastity; worse, this opinion had in course of time become prevalent among Christians, for second marriages had no blessing pronounced upon them and some Councils prohibited the clergy from being present on such occasions. The Apostle here condemns tyranny of that sort, and declares that no hindrance ought to be thrown in the way of widows marrying if they think proper. On the preference for widowhood he asks whether it is because widowhood is of itself a virtue, and answers no, but because it will have less to distract and is more exempt from earthly cares. On the last clause he denies that the expression means the apostle’s opinion was doubtful; it is as if he had said that such was his judgment on the question, for he immediately adds that he has the Spirit of God, which is sufficient to give full and perfect authority. He hears at the same time something of irony in the words, since the false apostles were ever and anon boasting in high-sounding terms of their having the Spirit of God for the purpose of arrogating authority to themselves, while endeavouring meanwhile to derogate from Paul’s; and so he says that he thinks he is not less a partaker of the Spirit than they.

Henry closes the whole chapter with advice to widows. As long as the husband lives the wife is bound by the law, confined to one husband and bound to continue and cohabit with him, and he notes that the marriage contract is for life, death only being able to annul the bond. But the husband being dead, she is at liberty to marry whom she will, there being no limitation by God’s law to be married only for such a number of times; and it is certain from this passage that second marriages are not unlawful, for otherwise the widow could not be at liberty to marry whom she pleased, nor to marry a second time at all, whereas the apostle asserts that she has such liberty when her husband is dead, only with the limitation that she marry in the Lord. From that limitation Henry draws a rule for all such decisions: in our choice of relations and change of conditions we should always have an eye to God, and marriages are likely to have God’s blessing only when they are made in the Lord, when persons are guided by the fear of God and the laws of God and act in dependence on the providence of God in the change and choice of a mate, when they can look up to God and sincerely seek his direction and humbly hope for his blessing upon their conduct. He observes that the apostle nevertheless calls her happier if she so abide, and reads that preference in the light of the whole chapter, as resting on the distress of the times and the freedom of the unmarried state from care rather than on any superior holiness in widowhood itself.

Clarke suspects that the opening words answer another question sent from Corinth, to this effect, whether a woman may remarry whose husband is dead or who has abandoned her; to which the apostle replies in general that as long as her husband is living the law binds her to him alone, but if the husband die she is free to remarry, only in the Lord. That limitation he presses further than the mere fact of Christian profession: she must not marry a heathen nor an irreligious man, and she should not only marry a genuine Christian but one of her own religious sentiments, for in reference to domestic peace much depends on this. On the closing preference he enters the sharpest caveat in the chapter, insisting that the words must be held to the present distress if consistency in the apostle’s reasoning is to be preserved, since otherwise it is hard to see how he could tell a widow that continuing in widowhood would be happier for her. She who had tried both the state of celibacy and the state of marriage could certainly best tell which was most for her comfort, and the apostle could say nothing about the future state of any widow except by an express revelation from heaven; it is certain that he can never be understood as speaking in general, since there are multitudes of persons abundantly more happy in their married than in their single state, and many widows also much more happy in their second marriage than they have been in their first. The judgment he takes as the view the apostle has of the subject by the light of the Divine Spirit, who shows him the tribulations coming on the Church, and he connects it with the earlier promise to spare them, the apostle declining to be more explicit concerning coming evils. Wesley states the limitation flatly, that only if Christians marry Christians is the direction satisfied, calling it a standing direction and one of the utmost importance. On the last clause he takes the opposite line from any reading that finds hesitation in it: the apostle claims the Spirit as well as any of them, teaching him all things, and this does not imply any doubt but the strongest certainty of it, together with a reproof of them for calling it in question. Whoever would conclude from the words that St Paul was not certain he had the Spirit of Christ neither understands their true import nor considers how expressly he lays claim to the Spirit both in this epistle and in the other; indeed it may be doubted whether the word here and elsewhere translated think does not always imply the fullest and strongest assurance.

Barnes takes the limitation to mean only to one who is a Christian, with a proper sense of her obligations to Christ and so as to promote his glory, holding that the apostle supposed this could not be done if she were allowed to marry a heathen or one of a different religion, the same sentiment being advanced in the second epistle, and that his intention was undoubtedly to affirm that it was proper for a widow to marry no one who was not a Christian. The reasons at that time he thinks obvious. They could have no sympathy and fellow-feeling on the most important of all subjects if the one was a Christian and the other a heathen. If she should marry a heathen, would it not show that she had not as deep a conviction of the importance and truth of her religion as she ought to have, since Christians were required to be separate, to be a peculiar people, and not to be conformed to the world, and these precepts could not be obeyed if the society of a heathen was voluntarily chosen and she became united to him for life. And she would in this way greatly hinder her own usefulness, putting herself in the control of one who had no respect for her religion. On the preference he takes it of remaining a widow even where she might be married to a Christian. On the last clause he weighs the verb carefully. Macknight and others suppose the phrase implies entire certainty, and that Paul means to affirm that here he was clear he was under the influence of inspiration, appealing for the use of the term to a string of passages; but Barnes answers that the word does not usually express absolute certainty, that it implies a doubt, though there may be a strong persuasion or conviction, or the best judgment which the mind can form in the case, and he cites his own string of passages in support. It implies here a belief that Paul was under the influence of the infallible Spirit and that his advice accorded with the will of God; and Barnes suspects an allusion to the fact that the teachers at Corinth deemed themselves to be under the influence of inspiration. Robertson notes that the phrase for the duration of the binding matches the language of the letter to the Romans, calls it the ideal and finds it pertinent today when husbands meet their former wives and wives meet their former husbands, remarking that there is a screw loose somewhere. He treats the remarriage of widows as a sort of addendum here, to be discussed again in the first letter to Timothy where younger widows are advised to marry, and observes that Paul leaves her free here also to be married again, only in the Lord, adding that every marriage ought to be in the Lord. He parses the aorist passive infinitive and the dative relative with unexpressed antecedent. On the preference he notes that the comparative is of the adjective used in the Beatitudes, that the word for judgment is the same used earlier in the chapter and is not a command, and that the verb for thinking differs from the one used a few verses before; but he insists that the apostle claims the Spirit of God in the expression of his inspired judgment on this difficult, complicated and tangled problem of marriage, having discharged his duty and leaving each one to decide for himself.

debates: What weight the closing I think carries: Barnes argues against Macknight that the verb does not usually express absolute certainty but a strong persuasion or the best judgment the mind can form, while Wesley holds it implies the fullest assurance and a reproof of those questioning it, Calvin denies any doubt and hears irony against the false apostles who boasted of the Spirit, and Robertson takes it as an inspired judgment rather than a command

How far only in the Lord restricts the choice: Barnes and Wesley confine it to marrying a Christian, Clarke presses further and would have her marry one of her own religious sentiments for the sake of domestic peace, and Robertson generalises it to every marriage whatever

Whether the widow is really happier unmarried: Clarke insists the judgment holds only for the present distress, since a woman who had tried both states could best tell and the apostle could know no widow’s future except by revelation, and points to multitudes happier married and widows happier in a second marriage, while Calvin denies that widowhood is a virtue in itself and grounds the preference solely on freedom from distraction
outliers: Calvin recalls that some Councils forbade the clergy to attend second marriages, and the chaplet of chastity given to once-married matrons
Robertson remarks that when former husbands and wives meet, there is a screw loose somewhere
Barnes and Calvin both suspect the Corinthian teachers’ claims to inspiration lie behind the last clause
